Kalyani had booked the seminar room for Thursday at four. The slides were due by noon, and Sangeeta had promised to finish the data section. At noon, nothing. At one, Kalyani texted, “How's it going?” Read, no reply. At three she started the section herself, her hands cold. At four, when the group gathered, Sangeeta strolled in with a coffee. “Oh, I didn't get to it. Sorry.”

Nobody said anything. Kalyani said, “It's fine.” It wasn't. It wasn't the missing slides; she could redo those. It was that Sangeeta had watched the hours go by and said nothing.

The next week Sangeeta promised to send the chart by Tuesday. Kalyani wrote the promise down but did not believe it.

qa.q: By what time were the slides due?
qa.a: The slides were due by noon.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when saying, “It's fine”?
qa.a: Kalyani felt disappointed and let down but held back, since the hurt was the silence, not the missing slides.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do before the next deadline?
qa.a: Kalyani could ask Sangeeta for a short progress check the day before and agree what to say if a task slips.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been thinking while letting the hours pass?
qa.a: Sangeeta may have felt embarrassed or overwhelmed and avoided saying so, hoping to catch up, without seeing how silence would hurt trust.

grounding: A group member is let down by another member who does not deliver and does not say so, and the silence makes future promises harder to believe.

“Jagdish, where's the summary?” Sabina asked. “It was due yesterday.”

“Uh... almost done.”

“You said that on Monday.”

“I was busy.”

Nita looked up from her laptop. “We waited for it before starting the slides. Now we have two hours.”

“I could have told you it was late,” said Jagdish.

“Yes,” said Sabina quietly. “That's the part that hurts more. I'd have started the summary myself if I'd known.”

“Okay. Sorry.”

“Next time just say, ‘I'm stuck.’ I can plan around stuck. I can't plan around silence.”

Jagdish nodded. Nita closed her laptop. “I'll believe you next time,” she said, “if you tell me early.”

qa.a: The summary was due yesterday.

qa.a: Sabina was hurt more by Jagdish's silence than by the delay, since hearing nothing made it impossible to plan or to trust future promises.

qa.a: Sabina asked Jagdish to say “I'm stuck” early, since Sabina can plan around stuck but not around silence.

qa.a: Nita probably feels frustrated and worried about time, having lost some trust in the timing.

passage:
The survey report for the kasba college was due on Monday. Ruchi and Tanvir had split it: she'd write the analysis, he'd bring the survey data from the two villages by Thursday.
Thursday came. No data. Ruchi messaged. Nothing. Friday, nothing. She saw him at the bus stand laughing with friends and he looked away.
On Sunday evening, he finally sent it. “Sorry, got delayed.”
Ruchi stayed up till two to finish. The data itself was fine. But sitting in the dim light, she realised she was more upset by the silence than by the delay. If he'd said on Thursday, she'd have planned.
Next month, when Tanvir said, “I'll do the charts,” she smiled, and quietly made her own backup.

qa.q: When was Tanvir supposed to bring the data?
qa.a: By Thursday.

qa.q: What was Ruchi feeling as she sat up till two?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and let down, more by Tanvir's silence than by the delay.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have done on Thursday to keep Ruchi's trust?
qa.a: He could have told her he was behind, so she could plan, instead of going silent.

qa.q: How might Tanvir have felt at the bus stand when he looked away?
qa.a: He was probably guilty and embarrassed, avoiding Ruchi because he hadn't delivered.

grounding: Shows a student let down by a teammate who misses a deadline without a word, where the silence makes future promises hard to believe.

At their university in Seoul, Jin and Nkechi were partners for the marketing project. Nkechi had promised the customer interviews by Wednesday.
Wednesday passed. Jin sent a message. Read, no reply. Thursday, the same. Jin saw her posting photos from a concert.
On Friday morning, Nkechi arrived with half the interviews. “Sorry, things got busy.”
Jin nodded, but his chest felt tight. The interviews weren't the problem; he could manage half. What bothered him was the two days of silence, the read receipts, the concert photos.
They finished on time. But the next week, when Nkechi said, “I'll handle the survey,” Jin heard himself say, “Let's check in daily,” and saw her face fall.

qa.q: How many of the interviews did Nkechi bring?
qa.a: She arrived with half the interviews.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when his chest felt tight?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and let down, bothered more by the two days of silence than by the half-done work.

qa.q: What could Nkechi do to rebuild Jin's trust?
qa.a: She could tell Jin early when she's behind and keep small promises, so her word becomes reliable again.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have felt when Jin asked for daily check-ins?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and a bit embarrassed, sensing he no longer fully trusts her.

grounding: Shows a student let down by a partner's silence after a missed deadline, which makes future promises harder to believe.

passage:
At 11 p.m. in the engineering lab, Siddharth stared at the shared folder. The data analysis Mehak had promised by Monday was still an empty file. It was Wednesday. The report was due Friday.
He had messaged on Monday night: "How's it going?" Mehak replied with a thumbs-up. Tuesday: "Need anything?" Nothing. Today she'd walked past him in the canteen, chatting with Tara and Rohit, and said nothing.
Siddharth wasn't even angry about the delay. People get sick; labs overrun. It was the thumbs-up. It meant he couldn't believe the next one.
At 11:40 Mehak finally texted: "Sorry. Totally stuck on the stats. Didn't want to admit it."
Siddharth read it twice. He typed, "We can fix stuck. I just need to know," and then, slowly, opened the file himself.

qa.q: By when had Mehak promised the data analysis?
qa.a: By Monday.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling about Mehak's thumbs-up?
qa.a: Siddharth felt let down and distrustful; the empty thumbs-up made any future promise from Mehak hard to believe.

qa.q: What could Mehak do differently next time she's stuck?
qa.a: Say so early, even just "I'm stuck on the stats", so the team can help before the deadline.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have stayed silent?
qa.a: Mehak was probably embarrassed and afraid of looking incapable, so hiding felt easier than admitting she was stuck.

grounding: Shows a team member let down by a teammate who missed a deadline without saying so, where the silence damages trust more than the delay.
